name: Quantum Subset Sum and k-SUM (Bernstein-Jeffery-Lange-Meurer; Chukhin-Kulikov-Levitskii-Mihajlin)
description: Quantum algorithms for worst-case Subset Sum and its parameterized k-SUM version. Bernstein, Jeffery, Lange and Meurer (PQCrypto 2013) gave the long-standing worst-case quantum upper bound O*(2^(n/3)) by splitting the input into three blocks, listing 2^(n/3) subset sums per block, and using quantum search / claw finding to match two lists against the third; the same paper also gave a heuristic O*(2^0.241n) random-instance algorithm combining Howgrave-Graham-Joux with a quantum-walk data structure on Johnson graphs. In 2026 Chukhin, Kulikov, Levitskii and Mihajlin replaced Wagner-style merging with a single four-block decomposition plus modular filtering by a random prime, obtaining a worst-case quantum k-SUM algorithm in time O~(n^{Psi_k}) with Psi_k = 2k/7 + O(1); instantiating it at k=7 and composing with the standard 7-block reduction yields an O*(2^(2n/7)) = O*(2^0.2857n) worst-case quantum algorithm for Subset Sum, improving the classical 2^(n/2) MITM baseline and the previous quantum 2^(n/3).
worst_case_time: Subset Sum: O*(2^(n/3)) worst-case (Bernstein-Jeffery-Lange-Meurer, 2013), improved to O*(2^(2n/7)) = O*(2^0.28571n) worst-case (Chukhin-Kulikov-Levitskii-Mihajlin, arXiv 2608.07309, Aug 2026) by reduction to worst-case 7-SUM. Worst-case k-SUM: O~(n^{Psi_k}) with Psi_k = (2k - floor(k/7) - floor((k+3)/7))/6 - [k=3 mod 7]/9 - [k=6 mod 7]/18, asymptotic to 2k/7 + O(1); this improves Tani's O~(n^{k/3}) for every k>3. For k=2, Ambainis (2007) gives O~(n^{2/3}). Pigeonhole Modular Equal Subset Sum: O*(2^(0.453n)) quantum by reduction to k-SUM.
space_complexity: Bernstein-Jeffery-Lange-Meurer's worst-case 3-block lookup algorithm stores a table of 2^k subset sums and uses O*(2^k) memory, balanced at k=n/3 (so O*(2^(n/3)) memory at the best time); the operation-count model may treat this as classical or quantum-accessible memory. Chukhin et al. use coherent dictionaries and a quantum walk and do not state a separate qubit/space bound. [uncertain]
model: Quantum circuit model with quantum random access to memory (qRAM / coherent dictionaries) for the data-structure layers; the worst-case BJLM lookup bound can be realized by a classical table accessed during quantum search, whereas the quantum-walk/Howgrave-Graham-Joux variant uses genuine quantum memory. Arithmetic is on O(log(sum of inputs))-bit integers. Non-quantum baselines referenced are word RAM. [uncertain]
randomized_or_deterministic: Bounded-error (Monte Carlo) quantum algorithms: quantum search, quantum walk (MNRS), amplitude amplification, phase estimation and Claw Finding give success probability at least 2/3 by standard amplification. Chukhin et al. additionally use a random prime and random m-element subsets, still with constant success probability; the guarantee is worst-case (over instances).
time_space_tradeoff_curve: BJLM's worst-case 3-block method is a tradeoff family: storing a table of 2^k sums (memory O*(2^k)) and quantum-searching the complementary 2^(n-k) choices in time O*(2^((n-k)/2)); balanced at k=n/3 gives O*(2^(n/3)) time and O*(2^(n/3)) memory. The simpler quantum MITM gives a 2^(n/3) time / 2^(n/3) space point. Chukhin et al. do not state a time-space tradeoff family (single point).
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: Worst-case Subset Sum quantum exponent: 1/3 = 0.33333 (Bernstein-Jeffery-Lange-Meurer, 2013); improved to 2/7 = 0.28571 (Chukhin-Kulikov-Levitskii-Mihajlin, Aug 2026). Random-instance quantum heuristic exponents reported: 0.241 (BJLM 2013 / Howgrave-Graham-Joux walk), 0.218 (BBSS 2020, as reported in arXiv:2608.07309), 0.1843 (Li 2025, heuristic ternary representation). Worst-case quantum k-SUM exponent Psi_k -> 2k/7.
problem_variant: Vanilla exact worst-case Subset Sum (arbitrary n integers and target); parameterized k-SUM (k lists of size n, pick one entry per list summing to target); Pigeonhole Modular Equal Subset Sum. The earlier random-instance results (Schrottenloher 2021, BBSS 2020, Li 2025) target single-solution random k-SUM/k-XOR.
applies_to: Exact feasibility/decision and search for arbitrary-input Subset Sum; k-SUM for all k>3 (Chukhin Theorem 1.2 improves Tani for every k>3); Pigeonhole Modular Equal Subset Sum (quantum O*(2^(0.453n))). The BJLM O*(2^(n/3)) result applies to worst-case (not merely random) inputs.
coefficient_set: C = {0,1} for Subset Sum. k-SUM selects exactly one element from each of k lists (an indicator vector with one 1 per list). Modular filtering works modulo a random prime p and keeps the canonical representative of each nonzero residue. Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum implicitly uses coefficients {-1,0,1} on two subsets.
density_regime: Density-agnostic for the worst-case quantum bounds (they hold for arbitrary integers of any density d = n/log2(max|a_i|)). The random-instance algorithms (HGJ/quantum-walk line: 0.241, 0.218, 0.1843) target random, density~1 instances.
solution_regime: Worst-case decision/search with no promise on the number of solutions (Chukhin et al. explicitly give a worst-case, not single-solution-random, guarantee). The single-solution random regime is the domain of the earlier Schrottenloher O~(n^{Phi_k}) bound.
cardinality_constraint: No fixed cardinality for Subset Sum; k is exactly the cardinality parameter for k-SUM (choose one entry from each of k lists, i.e. a star of k chosen indices), and the algorithm's four blocks have prescribed sizes 3k/14, 4k/14, 3k/14, 4k/14.
key_technique: BJLM 2^(n/3): split into three blocks, enumerate 2^(n/3) subset sums per block, and use quantum search / claw finding (Tani-style) to find a pair matching the third list. Their random-instance algorithm combines Howgrave-Graham-Joux with a streamlined quantum-walk data structure (quantum radix trees) on a product Johnson graph. Chukhin et al. 2026: group the k lists into four consecutive blocks (~3k/14, 4k/14, 3k/14, 4k/14); choose small m-element subsets S2, S4 of the two large blocks; filter by a random prime p=O~(m) keeping one canonical representative per residue bucket; run a quantum walk over pairs (S2,S4) to rebuild coherent dictionaries cheaply across neighbouring states; use quantum search for the left residue q and Claw Finding to match exact sums.
core_idea: Grover/quantum search gives a quadratic speedup over naive exhaustive search: if one block is enumerated into a table of 2^(n/3) sums, the complementary 2^(2n/3) candidates can be searched in time 2^((2n/3)/2) = 2^(n/3). The k-SUM advance avoids Wagner's merging tree (whose analysis needs the partial sums to be well distributed) by using a single four-block decomposition plus a random-prime modular filter: with constant probability the relevant block-2 and block-4 sums land in the canonical residue classes, so the filter isolates exact matches without distribution assumptions. The quantum walk keeps dictionary-update cost low when moving between neighbouring (S2,S4) states. Asymptotically Psi_k = 2k/7, so the 7-SUM-to-Subset-Sum block reduction gives exponent 2/7, the natural limit of this pipeline.
reduction_pipeline: Subset Sum -> k-SUM by the standard block reduction: partition n integers into k blocks, list all 2^(n/k) subset sums of each block, then solve the resulting k-SUM. Chukhin et al. instantiate k=7 (lists of size 2^(n/7)); their worst-case quantum 7-SUM runs in O~(n^2), giving O*(2^(2n/7)). Within k-SUM they reduce to an unbalanced 4-SUM plus modular filtering, solved by quantum search and Claw Finding. BJLM instead reduce Subset Sum to a 3-block (3-SUM) instance and apply quantum claw finding.
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive/algorithmic: the procedures return an explicit k-tuple of indices (a witness subset) with constant success probability; they are search algorithms, not existence proofs. Chukhin et al. state their algorithm 'solves' k-SUM, i.e. finds a solution.
search_vs_decision_witness: Returns an explicit witness (the chosen indices / subset); both feasibility (decision) and search are covered. The Pigeonhole Modular Equal Subset Sum application is also a search for two equal-sum subsets.
obstacle_to_2n3: For the quantum line the 2^(n/3) threshold is already surpassed (Chukhin et al. give 2^(2n/7) < 2^(n/3)); the precise remaining obstacle is going substantially below 2^(2n/7) toward 2^o(n). Within the 7-SUM pipeline the Subset Sum exponent is pinned to (1/7)*log2-time exponent of 7-SUM, and the best worst-case quantum k-SUM exponent is Psi_k ~ 2k/7, so one would need a better worst-case quantum k-SUM algorithm or a fundamentally different reduction; Tani's near-optimal claw-finding bound O~(n^{k/3}) limits the final matching primitive, and Wagner/merging-tree barriers constrain the random-instance techniques that do not give worst-case guarantees. For the classical target 2^(n/3), quantum speedups do not transfer to classical worst-case algorithms.
potential_to_break_mitm: High in the quantum model: both 2^(n/3) and 2^(2n/7) strictly beat the classical worst-case MITM baseline 2^(n/2) (and 2^(2n/7) beats the previous quantum record). Medium-to-low for pushing the quantum exponent far below 2/7 without a new worst-case quantum k-SUM breakthrough. This has essentially no bearing on whether the classical worst-case MITM barrier can be broken.
barrier_evidence: Tani (2009) gave a near-optimal quantum Claw Finding algorithm in O~(n^{k/3}) with a matching-type lower bound, so improvements must come from better reductions/structure rather than a faster claw-finding primitive. The classical k-SUM conjecture asserts meet-in-the-middle O~(n^{ceil(k/2)}) is optimal (its quantum analogue is less developed). Schrottenloher/Wagner-style merging trees face distribution and barrier constraints and only give random-instance guarantees. No unconditional quantum lower bound rules out 2^o(n) for Subset Sum; ETH/SETH give classical, not quantum, conditional lower bounds.
open_questions: Can the worst-case quantum k-SUM exponent be reduced below Psi_k (equivalently below 2k/7 + O(1))? Does a worst-case quantum Subset Sum algorithm in O*(2^(cn)) with c < 2/7 exist? Can the modular-filtering quantum walk be derandomized or made space-efficient? Are there quantum k-SUM or claw-finding lower bounds matching Psi_k? Can a better block reduction (e.g. unbalanced splits, 8-SUM, or output-sensitive quantum techniques) beat the 2^(2n/7) corollary? Does the quantum improvement have any consequence for the classical MITM barrier?
conditional_hypothesis: The upper bounds are unconditional. Contextual hardness: the classical k-SUM conjecture (hardness of O(n^{ceil(k/2)-eps})) and Tani's claw-finding lower bound constrain the building blocks; ETH/SETH constrain classical 2^o(n) algorithms but do not rule out 2^(2n/7) or a smaller constant exponent quantum algorithm.
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: The BJLM 2^(n/3) and Chukhin et al. 2^(2n/7) bounds are worst-case (arbitrary instances) with constant success probability. The exponents 0.241, 0.218 and 0.1843 are average-case/heuristic for random or single-solution instances. Schrottenloher's Phi_k bound is explicitly for single-solution random instances.
cryptographic_regime: Highly relevant to knapsack and subset-sum-based cryptanalysis: the algorithms attack 0/1 knapsack instances with n-bit values and target (density ~1 hard knapsacks in the BJLM framing). Quantum speedups set concrete key-size limits: an attack at 2^(cn) is feasible when cn bits fit in a quantum computer's budget. Elliptic-curve/discrete-log and post-quantum schemes are not directly affected, but knapsack/decoding-based proposals are. The 2013 paper is framed as attacking subset-sum cryptosystems.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: Largely orthogonal. Grover search and quantum walks accelerate search/matching steps quadratically but do not obviously compose with the FFT/convolution-based near-linear pseudopolynomial algorithms (Bringmann's O~(n+t), Chan's deterministic O~(t)) whose speed comes from algebraic convolution. Some works (e.g. Allcock-Hamoudi-Joux-Klingelhofer-Santha, arXiv:2111.07059) give quantum DP-based algorithms for subset-sum variants, indicating a potential but not yet exploited interaction.

empirical_evidence: None. These are asymptotic worst-case/average-case complexity results; no physical quantum-hardware demonstration of these exponents is reported.
implementation_artifact: none found (no code repository accompanies arXiv:2608.07309 or the BJLM paper; both provide pseudocode/algorithm descriptions only).
verification_method: Reproduce the proofs: (i) check the four-block sizes 3k/14, 4k/14, 3k/14, 4k/14 and the constant-probability modular-filtering lemma (a random prime p=O~(m) makes the relevant block-2/block-4 sums canonical); (ii) verify the quantum-walk update and mixing analysis for coherent dictionaries; (iii) verify the reduction arithmetic: Psi_7 = 2, so 7-SUM on lists of size 2^(n/7) costs (2^(n/7))^2 = 2^(2n/7), matching Corollary 1.3; (iv) compare Psi_k against Tani's k/3 and Schrottenloher's Phi_k for small k (e.g. Psi_3 = 8/9, Psi_6 = 16/9).
uncertain: the attribution that AHJ+22 attains the same O*(2^(n/3)) asymptotic bound for ordinary Subset Sum
